Den, der elsker det skønne, kaldes en elsker, fordi han har del i skønheden. For, som allerede sagt, har hver menneskesjæl af natur skuet det sande væsen — dette var betingelsen for hendes overgang til menneskeskikkelse. Men ikke alle sjæle minder let de ting fra den anden verden. englishChanges.before: And not only is he mischievous and unpleasant while his love lasts — when his love is over, he becomes a treacherous enemy to the very person on whom he showered oaths, prayers, and promises, and who could barely be induced even then to tolerate the tedium of his company out of self-interest. The oyster-shell has fallen the other way up; he turns from pursuit to flight, while the other is left chasing him with passion and curses, not realizing he should never have accepted a deranged lover instead of a sensible non-lover in the first place. englishChanges.before: It will be more to the point to appeal to the ancient inventors of names, who would never have linked prophecy (mantike), the noblest of arts that foretells the future, with madness (manike), calling them both by the same name, if they had thought madness a disgrace or dishonor. They must have believed there was an inspired madness which was something noble — for the two words, mantike and manike, are really the same, and the letter tau is only a modern and tasteless addition. And this is confirmed by the name they gave to the rational investigation of the future, whether by birds or other signs. Because that investigation supplies mind (nous) and information (istoria) from the reasoning faculty to human thought (oiesis), they originally called it oionoistike. The word has lately been altered and made sonorous by the modern insertion of the letter Omega (oionoistike to oionistike). And just as prophecy (mantike) is more perfect and august than augury, in both name and fact, so — as the ancients testify — madness is superior to a sane mind (sophrosune): for the one is of human origin only, the other of divine. Again, where plagues and the heaviest miseries have arisen in certain families because of some ancient blood-guilt, madness has entered with holy prayers and rites, and through inspired utterances has found deliverance for those in need. Whoever shares this gift, being truly possessed and properly out of his mind, is made whole by purifications and mysteries, freed from evil present and future, and released from the calamity afflicting him. The third kind is the madness of those possessed by the Muses — which, taking hold of a delicate and virgin soul, kindles a frenzy in it, awakening lyric poetry and every other kind of song. With these the soul adorns the countless deeds of ancient heroes for the instruction of posterity. But anyone who comes to the temple door without a touch of the Muses' madness in his soul, supposing he'll get inside by craft alone — he and his poetry are not admitted. The sane man vanishes and is nowhere to be seen when he enters into competition with the madman.

englishChanges.before: The soul in her whole being is immortal, for whatever is ever in motion is immortal. But that which moves another and is moved by another, ceasing to move, also ceases to live. Only the self-moving, never leaving itself, never ceases to move, and is the fountain and origin of motion in everything else that moves. The origin is unbegotten, since whatever is begotten has an origin — but the origin itself is begotten of nothing, for if it were begotten of something, then what is begotten would not come from an origin. And if unbegotten, it must also be indestructible: for if the origin were destroyed, nothing could ever again come out of anything, nor anything come out of an origin — and everything must have an origin. So the self-moving is the origin of motion, and this can be neither destroyed nor begotten, or else the whole heavens and all creation would collapse and stand still, never to have motion or birth again. But if the self-moving is shown to be immortal, anyone who affirms that self-motion is the very idea and essence of the soul will not be embarrassed. For the body that is moved from outside is soulless; but that which is moved from within has a soul, since such is the nature of the soul. And if this is true, must not the soul be the self-moving, and therefore necessarily unbegotten and immortal? Enough on the soul's immortality.

englishChanges.before: Ten thousand years must pass before each soul can return to the place from which she came, for she cannot grow her wings again in less time — except the soul of a guileless and true philosopher, or the soul of a lover who is not devoid of philosophy: these may regain their wings in the third of the thousand-year periods, distinguished from the ordinary good man who gains his wings in three thousand years. Those who choose this life three times in succession are given wings and depart at the end of three thousand years. But the others receive judgment when they have completed their first life. After judgment, some go to the houses of correction beneath the earth and are punished; others are lightly borne by justice to some place in heaven and live there in a manner worthy of the life they led on earth in human form. At the end of the first thousand years both the good souls and the evil come to draw lots and choose their second life, and they may take any they please. The soul of a man may pass into the life of a beast, or from a beast return again into a man. But the soul that has never seen truth will never pass into human form. For a man must have understanding of universals, and be able to proceed from the many particulars of sense to a single conception of reason — this is the recollection of those things our soul once saw when following God, when, ignoring what we now call being, she raised her head toward true being. So the mind of the philosopher alone has wings — and rightly: he is always, to the measure of his ability, clinging in recollection to those things in which God abides, and in beholding which God is what He is. The man who rightly uses these memories is forever being initiated into perfect mysteries, and alone becomes truly perfect. But because he forgets earthly interests and is rapt in the divine, the vulgar consider him mad and rebuke him — not seeing that he is inspired.

englishChanges.before: So far I have been speaking of the fourth and last kind of madness — the kind attributed to a man who, when he sees the beauty of earth, is transported by the recollection of true beauty. He longs to fly away, but cannot; he is like a bird fluttering and looking upward, careless of the world below — and so he is thought mad. I have shown this to be the noblest and highest of all inspirations, and the offspring of the highest, to whoever has or shares in it. The one who loves the beautiful is called a lover because he partakes of beauty. For, as already said, every human soul has by nature beheld true being — this was the condition of her passing into human form. But not all souls easily recall the things of the other world. They may have seen them for only a short time, or they may have been unfortunate in their earthly lot and, having had their hearts turned toward unrighteousness through some corrupting influence, have lost the memory of the holy things they once saw. Only a few retain an adequate remembrance, and when they here behold any image of that other world, they are rapt in amazement — though they don't know what their rapture means, because they do not perceive clearly. For there is no light of justice or temperance or any of the higher ideas which are precious to souls in the earthly copies of them: these are seen through a glass dimly, and there are only a few who, going to the images, behold in them the realities, and these only with difficulty. There was a time when, with the rest of the happy band, we saw beauty shining in brightness — we philosophers following in the train of Zeus, others in company with other gods. Then we beheld the beatific vision and were initiated into a mystery that may truly be called most blessed, celebrated by us in our state of innocence, before we had any experience of the evils to come, when we were admitted to the sight of apparitions innocent and simple and calm and happy, which we beheld shining in pure light — pure ourselves, and not yet enshrined in this living tomb we carry about now that we are imprisoned in the body like an oyster in its shell. Let me linger over the memory of scenes long passed away.

englishChanges.before: As I said at the beginning of this tale, I divided each soul into three — two horses and a charioteer; and one of the horses was good and the other bad. The division may stand, but I have not yet explained what the goodness or badness of either consists in, and to that I'll now proceed. The right-hand horse is upright and cleanly built; he has a lofty neck and an aquiline nose; his color is white and his eyes are dark; he is a lover of honor and modesty and temperance, and a follower of true glory. He needs no touch of the whip, but is guided by word and admonition alone. The other is a crooked, lumbering animal, thrown together anyhow. He has a short thick neck; he is flat-faced and dark-colored, with gray and blood-shot eyes; the mate of insolence and pride, shaggy-eared and deaf, scarcely yielding to whip and spur. Now when the charioteer beholds the vision of love, and his whole soul is warmed through sense, and is full of the prickings and ticklings of desire, the obedient horse, then as always governed by shame, refrains from leaping on the beloved. But the other, heedless of the pricks and the blows of the whip, plunges and runs away, giving every kind of trouble to his companion and the charioteer, whom he forces to approach the beloved and remember the joys of love. They at first indignantly resist him and will not be driven to do terrible and unlawful deeds. But at last, when he persists in plaguing them, they yield and agree to do as he bids. And now they are at the spot and behold the flashing beauty of the beloved — which, when the charioteer sees, his memory is carried back to true beauty, whom he beholds in company with Modesty like an image placed on a holy pedestal. He sees her, but he is afraid and falls backward in adoration, and by his fall is compelled to pull back the reins with such violence that he brings both horses on their haunches — the one willing and unresisting, the unruly one very unwilling. When they have gone back a little, the one is overcome with shame and wonder, his whole soul bathed in sweat. The other, when the pain caused by the bridle and the fall is over and he has with difficulty caught his breath, is full of wrath and reproaches, which he heaps on the charioteer and his fellow-horse for cowardice and lack of manliness, accusing them of breaking their agreement and deserting. Again they refuse, and again he urges them on, and will scarcely yield to their plea that he wait until another time. When the appointed hour comes, they pretend to have forgotten, and he reminds them, fighting and neighing and dragging them on, until at last he, intent on the same thoughts, forces them to draw near again. And when they are near he stoops his head and puts up his tail and takes the bit in his teeth and pulls shamelessly. Then the charioteer is worse off than ever; he falls back like a racer at the barrier, and with a still more violent wrench drags the bit out of the wild horse's teeth, covering his abusive tongue and jaws with blood, forcing his legs and haunches to the ground and punishing him sorely. And when this has happened several times and the villain has ceased from his wanton behavior, he is tamed and humbled, and follows the will of the charioteer; and when he sees the beautiful one, he is ready to die of fear. From that time forward, the soul of the lover follows the beloved in modesty and holy fear.
